basic_information.name: RAGFlow
basic_information.creator: InfiniFlow (Shanghai, China), an AI infrastructure and service provider committed to democratizing AI technology
basic_information.description: RAGFlow is a leading open-source Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) engine built on deep document understanding. It combines template-based chunking, hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector + cross-encoder reranking), and agentic workflow capabilities into a unified platform with a visual no-code canvas. Its standout feature is the DeepDoc parsing engine, which understands document structure (tables, headers, charts, footnotes) rather than naively splitting text, producing higher-quality chunks for retrieval. With 73K+ GitHub stars and 1M+ Docker Hub pulls, RAGFlow is one of the most popular open-source RAG platforms, especially strong for enterprises needing to process complex document formats (PDFs, scanned images, legal contracts, scientific papers) with traceable, citation-grounded answers.
basic_information.release_date: Open-sourced April 1, 2024; latest stable version v0.23.1 (January 2026)

technical_architecture.architecture_type: Microservices architecture deployed via Docker Compose. Separates frontend presentation, API layer (Flask-based, upgraded to async in v0.23+), core processing engine (DeepDoc for document parsing, embedding pipeline, retrieval pipeline), and infrastructure services (Elasticsearch or Infinity for document/vector storage, Redis for caching, MinIO for object storage). Supports both Elasticsearch and InfiniFlow's own Infinity AI-native database as storage backends. Infinity compiles queries into a computational DAG for pipelined execution, outperforming Elasticsearch for vector search workloads.
technical_architecture.language: Python (primary backend, Flask web framework), TypeScript/JavaScript (frontend React-based UI), with Infinity database core in C++. Docker-based deployment. Python SDK and REST APIs for programmatic access.
technical_architecture.embedding_dimensions: Supports arbitrary embedding dimensions depending on the chosen embedding model. Compatible with all major embedding model outputs (384, 768, 1024, 1536, 3072+). Built-in support for BCE, BGE, Jina, and Qwen embedding models, plus any OpenAI-API-compatible embedding endpoint.
technical_architecture.indexing_algorithm: Hybrid indexing: full-text inverted index (BM25) via Elasticsearch or Infinity, plus dense vector index (HNSW) for semantic search. When using Infinity backend, benefits from optimized fused ranking that combines full-text and vector search in a single query pipeline (3-5x faster than separate queries). Elasticsearch provides standard BM25 + kNN vector search.
technical_architecture.scalability: Designed for enterprise-scale document processing. Minimum requirements: 4 CPU cores, 16GB RAM, 50GB disk. Supports processing large document collections with configurable parallelism. Infinity backend outperforms Elasticsearch for large-scale vector workloads. Horizontal scaling via Kubernetes is community-requested but not officially supported via Helm charts yet; primary deployment is single-node Docker Compose. Multi-tenancy supported via team management (added v0.14.0+).
technical_architecture.deployment_options: Docker Compose (primary, x86 only with slim editions from v0.22.0+), GPU-accelerated Docker images for DeepDoc tasks, source code deployment for development. Kubernetes deployment possible but no official Helm charts. Third-party managed hosting available via Elest.io. No official cloud-managed SaaS offering from InfiniFlow. gVisor optional for sandboxed code execution.

rag_specific_capabilities.retrieval_method: Hybrid retrieval combining dense vector search (cosine similarity via HNSW) and sparse keyword search (BM25). Candidate chunks are retrieved separately by both methods, then merged into a unified pool. Cross-encoder reranking model (from Sentence Transformers library) evaluates query-chunk pairs for contextual relevance scoring. Built-in reranking models include BCE, BGE, Jina, and BAAI rerankers. Supports multi-recall with fused ranking for enhanced precision and recall.
rag_specific_capabilities.chunking_strategy_support: Template-based chunking is RAGFlow's signature feature. Multiple built-in templates: General (universal), Q&A (question-answer pairs), Manual (user-defined), Table (structured tabular data), Paper (academic papers), Book (long-form text with chapters), Laws (legal documents with article/clause structure), Presentation (slide decks). The DeepDoc engine uses OCR, layout recognition, and document structure models to intelligently segment documents according to their inherent structure rather than arbitrary character counts. Users select template per dataset. Long-context RAG (v0.21.0+) automatically generates document-level table of contents (TOC) structures to mitigate context loss from inaccurate chunking.
rag_specific_capabilities.reranking_support: Built-in cross-encoder reranking via Sentence Transformers. Supports BCE, BGE, Jina, and BAAI reranker models. Fused ranking combines BM25 and vector search scores before reranking. Reranking significantly improves true positive retrievals while reducing false positives. Users can configure reranking model choice per dataset.
rag_specific_capabilities.multimodal_support: Strong multimodal document processing via DeepDoc engine: handles images, tables, charts within documents using OCR and layout recognition. Supports scanned documents and image-based PDFs. Parses tables into structured data. Chart and figure extraction with caption association. Audio input/output support added for Agent interactions. MDX file parsing support added in recent versions. Does not natively support video embeddings.
rag_specific_capabilities.graph_rag_support: Built-in GraphRAG support since v0.12.0. Users can select 'Knowledge Graph' as chunking method for a knowledge base and define entity types (organization, person, location, etc.) for LLM-based extraction. LLM-powered deduplication handles synonyms (e.g., '2024' vs 'Year 2024'). Visual display of knowledge graphs with node names, descriptions, and communities, including mind map view. Current limitation: knowledge graph construction is at the document level only; cannot link knowledge graphs across multiple documents within a knowledge base.
rag_specific_capabilities.citation_grounding: Built-in citation and grounding system is a core differentiator. RAGFlow provides traceable references with visualized text chunking, allowing users to see exactly which chunks were retrieved and how they contributed to the answer. Reduces hallucinations by grounding responses in specific document passages. Users can visually inspect and verify the chunking and retrieval results, making the RAG process explainable and auditable.
rag_specific_capabilities.context_window_optimization: Long-context RAG (introduced v0.21.0) automatically generates document-level table of contents (TOC) structures, enabling retrieval at multiple granularity levels and mitigating context loss caused by inaccurate or excessive chunking. Orchestrable ingestion pipeline allows customized data flow templates to optimize what enters the context window. Users can configure chunk sizes and overlap per template. Agent memory module (v0.23.0) enables selective context retrieval from conversation history.

performance_and_benchmarks.latency: No official p50/p99 latency benchmarks published. Agent processing time reduced by approximately 50% in v0.23.0 compared to initial Agent release in v0.20.0. Flask framework upgraded from synchronous to asynchronous in v0.23.0, increasing concurrency and preventing blocking issues. When using Infinity backend, query performance is 3-5x faster than Elasticsearch for fused search operations. [uncertain]
performance_and_benchmarks.throughput: No official QPS benchmarks published. Asynchronous Flask upgrade improves concurrent request handling. Document processing throughput depends on document complexity, chosen parsing template, and whether GPU acceleration is enabled for DeepDoc tasks. Infinity backend offers higher throughput than Elasticsearch for combined vector + full-text queries. [uncertain]
performance_and_benchmarks.accuracy_metrics: No published MTEB, BEIR, or standardized RAG benchmark scores. RAGFlow's accuracy depends on the chosen embedding model, chunking template, and reranking model. The deep document understanding approach (structure-aware parsing) is claimed to produce higher-quality chunks than naive chunking, leading to better retrieval relevance. GraphRAG provides more comprehensive answers for multi-hop queries involving nested logic. [uncertain]
performance_and_benchmarks.benchmark_results: No standardized benchmark results published for RAGFlow as a complete system. Infinity database (backend) has official benchmarks showing it outperforms all known open-source vector databases for vector search, with 3-5x improvement in fused query performance in v0.5.0. Infinity benchmark suite supports comparison against Qdrant, Elasticsearch, and Quickwit across gist, sift, geonames, enwiki, and tantivy datasets. [uncertain]

integration_and_ecosystem.framework_compatibility: RAGFlow operates as a self-contained RAG platform rather than a component library, so integration with LangChain/LlamaIndex is primarily via its REST API and Python SDK rather than as a native vector store plugin. Provides HTTP API for integration into existing application stacks. Supports webhook triggering for Agent outputs. Agent canvas enables building workflows that can incorporate external tools. Not a drop-in LangChain VectorStore or LlamaIndex VectorStoreIndex replacement — it is a full-stack RAG application.
integration_and_ecosystem.model_compatibility: Extensive LLM provider support: OpenAI (GPT-4, GPT-5 series), Anthropic (Claude 4), Google (Gemini 3 Pro), DeepSeek (R1, V3), Qwen/Tongyi-Qianwen, and any OpenAI-API-compatible endpoint. Local model deployment via Ollama and Xinference. Embedding models: BCE, BGE, Jina, Qwen 3 Embedding, plus any OpenAI-compatible embedding API. Reranking models: BCE, BGE, Jina, BAAI rerankers. Configuration via web UI Model Providers page.
integration_and_ecosystem.mcp_integration_status: Official MCP (Model Context Protocol) server available since mid-2025. Published on PyPI as ragflow-mcp-server. Supports both legacy SSE transport (/sse, deprecated March 2025) and streamable-HTTP transport (/mcp). Two deployment modes: self-host (single API key, access specific tenant datasets) and host mode (per-client API keys, each client accesses own datasets). Enables RAGFlow integration with Claude, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible AI agents. MCP tools can list datasets, create chat assistants, and manage conversations.
integration_and_ecosystem.data_source_connectors: Built-in data synchronization from: AWS S3 (with role-based authentication), Google Drive, Notion, Confluence, Discord, and JIRA. Supports direct file upload for: Word, PowerPoint, Excel, PDF, images, scanned documents, text files, MDX, and web pages. MinIO support for S3-compatible storage. Orchestrable ingestion pipeline (v0.21.0+) allows customized data flow templates on the canvas. No native Slack connector as of February 2026.
integration_and_ecosystem.observability_integration: Native Langfuse integration for observability and tracing. Langfuse automatically captures detailed traces and metrics for every RAGFlow request, supporting interactive UI runs, scheduled jobs, and API calls. Configuration available in RAGFlow API settings. Through Langfuse's OpenTelemetry foundation, traces can also be forwarded to Datadog or other monitoring platforms. No native LangSmith integration documented. No built-in Prometheus metrics or Grafana dashboards. [uncertain]

pricing_and_cost.pricing_model: Fully open-source (Apache 2.0) with no proprietary tiers or paid cloud service from InfiniFlow. Self-hosted only. No per-query, per-vector, or per-seat pricing. Third-party managed hosting available via Elest.io (starts at $58/month for smallest instance). Cost is purely infrastructure (compute, storage, GPU if used for DeepDoc).
pricing_and_cost.free_tier: Entirely free and open-source. No feature gating or usage limits in the open-source version. All features (GraphRAG, Agent, MCP, all templates, all model integrations) available in the free version.
pricing_and_cost.cost_at_scale: Infrastructure costs only. Minimum requirements: 4 CPU cores, 16GB RAM, 50GB disk. A mid-range VM ($50-150/month) can handle moderate document collections. GPU acceleration for DeepDoc parsing (layout recognition, OCR) increases processing speed but adds cost ($0.50-3/hour for GPU instances). Elasticsearch or Infinity storage costs scale with document volume. Embedding and LLM API costs are external (e.g., OpenAI API charges). Elest.io managed hosting: $58-300+/month depending on instance size. [uncertain]
pricing_and_cost.total_cost_of_ownership: Self-hosted: $0 software licensing + $50-300/month infrastructure for small-to-medium deployments. Add GPU costs if using DeepDoc acceleration ($100-500+/month). External LLM API costs depend on usage volume and provider (e.g., $0.50-5/1M tokens for OpenAI). Embedding generation costs if using API-based models. Ops overhead is moderate: Docker Compose deployment is straightforward, but no official Kubernetes support means scaling requires manual effort. No commercial support contract available from InfiniFlow. [uncertain]

adoption_and_market.market_position: Leading open-source RAG framework by GitHub stars (~73K), positioning it as the most starred dedicated RAG engine globally. Strong in the document-heavy RAG niche, differentiated by deep document understanding capabilities. Competes in the broader 'RAG platform' space alongside Dify, Langflow, and Haystack. Particularly popular in the Chinese tech ecosystem due to InfiniFlow's Shanghai base and strong Chinese LLM integration (Qwen, DeepSeek). Emerging challenger in the Western market.
adoption_and_market.notable_customers: No specific enterprise customer names publicly documented. Positioned for enterprise adoption with multi-tenancy, team management, and API access. Strong community adoption among developers building document-heavy RAG applications (legal, financial, academic, healthcare document processing). Listed in DeepSeek's official awesome-deepseek-integration repository. [uncertain]
adoption_and_market.community_size: ~73,000 GitHub stars, ~8,100 forks, 1M+ Docker Hub pulls, 64 Docker Hub stars. Active Medium blog by InfiniFlow team. X/Twitter presence at @infiniflowai. Community-driven with open GitHub issue tracker. Discord/Slack community size not publicly documented. Rapid growth trajectory: from 0 to 26K stars in first 8 months (April-December 2024), then to 73K by February 2026.
adoption_and_market.funding_and_valuation: InfiniFlow has received investment from Capital X (China) and Chenhui Venture Partners. Specific funding amounts, round designations, and valuation not publicly disclosed as of February 2026. Company founded in 2023 and headquartered in Shanghai. PitchBook and Crunchbase profiles exist but detailed financial data is behind paywalls. [uncertain]
adoption_and_market.competitive_landscape: Direct competitors in the RAG platform space: Dify (easier UI, broader LLM app development, less deep document parsing), Langflow (visual no-code builder, lighter-weight, less document-focused), Haystack (more developer-oriented, pipeline-as-code approach). Document processing competitors: Unstructured.io, LlamaParse. Infrastructure competitors: LangChain + vector DB combinations. Key differentiators: (1) deepest document understanding via DeepDoc engine, (2) template-based chunking with visual inspection, (3) built-in citation grounding and explainability, (4) Infinity database as purpose-built RAG backend, (5) strongest GraphRAG integration among open-source RAG platforms.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Best for: teams of 2-15 building document-centric AI products (legal tech, fintech document analysis, healthcare records, academic research tools, enterprise knowledge bases). Ideal when document quality and structure matter more than raw speed-to-market. Budget: $0 for software + $50-300/month infrastructure. Use case fit: any application where complex documents (PDFs with tables, scanned images, multi-column layouts, legal contracts) need to be accurately parsed and queried. Not recommended for: simple chatbot MVPs (Dify is faster to deploy), teams without Docker experience, pure text-only use cases where naive chunking suffices, or teams needing a fully managed cloud service.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy_guidance: Self-host (only option from InfiniFlow): when team has Docker/DevOps capability, needs full control over data processing pipeline, and deals with complex document formats. Use Elest.io managed hosting when: team lacks DevOps resources but needs RAGFlow's document processing capabilities. Consider alternatives when: need a managed cloud RAG service (use Pinecone + LlamaIndex), need rapid prototyping without infrastructure (use Dify Cloud), or need a code-first approach (use LangChain + vector DB directly). Migration consideration: RAGFlow is a full-stack platform, so migrating away requires rebuilding the document processing pipeline, not just swapping a vector store.
entrepreneurial_relevance.time_to_production: POC: 1-3 days (Docker Compose deployment + upload documents + test queries via web UI). MVP with customized templates: 1-2 weeks (template tuning, embedding model selection, LLM configuration). Production deployment: 3-6 weeks including document pipeline optimization, agent workflow design, API integration, and performance tuning. The visual web UI accelerates initial setup, but production-grade document processing (especially with custom templates or GraphRAG) requires iteration. Learning curve is steeper than Dify but shallower than building from scratch with LangChain.
key_lessons: 1. Document structure awareness is a competitive moat — RAGFlow's template-based chunking produces dramatically better results than naive character-splitting for complex documents. If your startup processes PDFs with tables, multi-column layouts, or mixed media, this deep document understanding is the difference between a demo that works and a product that works.

2. Choose your storage backend deliberately — Elasticsearch is the safe default with broad community support, but Infinity offers 3-5x better fused search performance. Start with Elasticsearch for familiarity, benchmark against Infinity when performance matters, and switch if the gains justify the lesser ecosystem support.

3. Visual chunk inspection builds user trust — RAGFlow's ability to show users exactly which document chunks generated an answer (with citations) is a powerful product feature for enterprise customers who need auditability. Build this into your product demo early.

4. GraphRAG is powerful but limited — document-level knowledge graphs enable impressive multi-hop reasoning demos, but the current limitation of no cross-document graph linking means it works best for deep single-document analysis rather than corpus-wide knowledge discovery. Plan your product claims accordingly.

5. Budget for GPU infrastructure if processing scanned documents — DeepDoc's layout recognition and OCR capabilities are RAGFlow's killer feature, but they benefit significantly from GPU acceleration. Factor $100-500/month GPU costs into your unit economics if your use case involves scanned or image-heavy documents.
entrepreneurial_relevance.no_code_interface: Yes — RAGFlow provides a full visual web interface for document management, RAG workflow creation, dataset configuration, template selection, and agent orchestration. The canvas-based workflow builder (v0.20.0+) enables no-code design of agentic and RAG pipelines with drag-and-drop components. Multi-Agent support allows multiple agents on a single canvas. Non-technical users can upload documents, select chunking templates, preview chunks visually, and create chat assistants without writing code.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 2 (Prompt engineering & no-code tools — hands-on RAG demo with visual interface), Session 3 (Framing & managing AI projects — document processing pipeline design, template selection decisions, Build vs Buy for RAG infrastructure)

confidence.data_quality: High — information sourced from official RAGFlow GitHub repository (73K stars), RAGFlow official website and documentation, InfiniFlow Medium blog posts, official release notes, PyPI (ragflow-mcp-server), Docker Hub statistics, and multiple independent comparison articles from Firecrawl, Sider.ai, MarkTechPost, and Bestarion.
confidence.cross_reference: GitHub stars and version history confirmed via GitHub. Docker Hub pulls (1M+) confirmed via Docker Hub. MCP server confirmed via PyPI and official RAGFlow docs. Deep document understanding and template-based chunking confirmed across GitHub README, official docs, MarkTechPost, and multiple Medium articles. GraphRAG support confirmed via official RAGFlow blog post and documentation. Langfuse integration confirmed via Langfuse official integrations page.
confidence.caveats: No official performance benchmarks published for RAGFlow as a complete system (only Infinity database has benchmarks). Funding details for InfiniFlow are not publicly available in detail. No specific enterprise customer names are publicly documented. Kubernetes support is community-requested but not officially provided via Helm charts. The project iterates rapidly (v0.1 to v0.23 in under 2 years), which means API stability may be a concern for production deployments. Chinese-language documentation and community may be more comprehensive than English resources. CVE-2025-68700 and CVE-2025-69286 have been reported, indicating active security scrutiny but also real vulnerabilities.
confidence.security_posture: Two CVEs reported in 2025 (CVE-2025-68700, CVE-2025-69286), indicating the platform has faced real security vulnerabilities. As an open-source self-hosted platform, security depends on deployment configuration. No SOC 2 or HIPAA certification. GDPR compliance is the deployer's responsibility. RAG-specific attack surfaces apply: knowledge base poisoning (adversarial document injection), prompt injection via retrieved content, and potential data leakage through retrieval results. Role-based authentication for S3 access added for data connector security. gVisor sandboxing available for code execution. No documented embedding inversion protections. Users should follow standard container security practices and network isolation for production deployments.
